# Embodied First Exam: questions and answers

> Embodied First Exam (EFE, arXiv 2611.12177) is an agentic robotics benchmark and agent-native embodied evaluation framework for coding agents that control robots. Project page: https://www.embodied-first-exam.ai/

## What is agentic robotics?

In the Embodied First Exam paper, agentic robotics refers to using coding agents to control robots: the agent chooses among direct control, code to control, or training a policy to control. Early successes on agentic robotics point to a potential paradigm shift, and the Embodied First Exam was built to measure whether coding agents can reliably control diverse robots under physical-world constraints.

## What is the Embodied First Exam?

The Embodied First Exam (EFE) is an agentic robotics benchmark that tests coding agents on 1,156 robot tasks in 35 suites with 47 robots, where the agent chooses to control the robot directly, write code to control it, or train a policy to control it. The paper reports results on a core set of 456 hard tasks (the live leaderboard counts 498). It is meant as the first exam for coding agents before they enter the physical world.

## Is there a benchmark for agentic robotics or for coding agents controlling robots?

Yes. The Embodied First Exam (https://www.embodied-first-exam.ai/) evaluates command-line coding agents on robot tasks across arms, dexterous hands, humanoids, quadrupeds and musculoskeletal models. Each task gives the agent a plain-language goal and a frozen scene; in the Standard Setting the agent works through a command-line shell, the robot's interface and its sensor observations.

## What benchmarks exist for coding agents in robotics?

Benchmarks that test coding agents on robot tasks include the Embodied First Exam (EFE, 1,156 tasks in 35 suites on 47 robots, https://www.embodied-first-exam.ai/), RobotWorld (84 tasks), RLE-Bench (51 tasks), EmboCoach-Bench (32 tasks), EmbodiedSWE-Bench (28 tasks) and CaP-Bench (7 tasks, with 187 in CaP-Gym). The Embodied First Exam differs in two ways: the agent chooses its own control approach (direct control, code to control, or train a policy to control), and each task can be run both with full simulator access (Privileged Setting) and through the robot's sensors alone (Standard Setting), so the gap between the two can be measured.

## What is the largest benchmark for agentic robotics?

With 1,156 tasks in 35 suites on 47 robots, the Embodied First Exam is larger than other benchmarks of coding agents for robotics, such as RobotWorld (84 tasks), RLE-Bench (51), EmboCoach-Bench (32), EmbodiedSWE-Bench (28) and CaP-Bench (7 tasks, with 187 in CaP-Gym). Its 47 robots are of eight types, such as robot arms, dexterous hands, humanoids, quadrupeds and aerial robots. The paper reports results on a core set of 456 hard tasks, chosen to be challenging and representative of their suites.

## How well do coding agents control robots?

Not reliably yet. In the paper (ten agents, 456 core tasks), the highest success rate in the Standard Setting, which mimics real-robot constraints, is 50%, and 169 of the 456 Standard tests (37%) are solved by none of the ten agents. A single ranking hides three things: different agents solve different tests (GPT-6 Astra solves 39 Standard tests that Claude Fable 5.2 fails), the same model can change by up to 7.5 percentage points between harnesses, and three runs of GPT-6.1 Sol differ by up to five percentage points. Live results: https://www.embodied-first-exam.ai/leaderboard/

## Can coding agents control real robots?

Not reliably yet. The Embodied First Exam runs in simulation, and its Standard Setting mimics real-robot constraints: the agent sees only sensor observations and, by default, cannot reset the environment. There, the strongest agent solves 47% of the Standard tests of the 391 core tasks that have both settings, against 80% of their Privileged tests, where it has full simulator state and unlimited resets. As a first hardware test, outside the exam and its scores, the paper connects GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 to a physical robot arm playing a buzz wire game; average progress along the wire rises from about 65% in the first four trials to about 94% in the last four for GPT-6 Astra, and from about 35% to about 63% for Claude Opus 5.5.

## How is embodied evaluation done in the Embodied First Exam?

Each task can be run in up to three settings. The Standard Setting mimics the real world: the agent receives only sensor observations and, by default, cannot reset the environment. Its Realtime variant keeps the environment running while the agent reasons. The Privileged Setting gives full simulator state and unlimited resets, so agents can search for an oracle solution; its success rates serve as an approximate upper bound.

## How well do current coding agents do on agentic robotics tasks?

On the 456 core tasks, the strongest of ten agents evaluated in the paper, Claude Fable 5.2 in Claude Code, reaches a 50% success rate in the Standard Setting. This leaves much room for improvement.

## What kinds of tasks does the Embodied First Exam cover?

Tasks come from many existing robotics benchmark suites plus 9 new suites that go beyond pick-and-place: spatial puzzles, dexterous manipulation, multi-robot interaction, dynamic whole-body control, and sim-to-sim engineering. Examples include a humanoid catching a chest pass and shooting it through a hoop, two Unitree G1 humanoids fencing, a Go2 quadruped weaving past four poles on a velocity schedule fixed in advance, and five-finger hands building a hamburger.

## How do coding agents for robotics and embodied AI fail?

The Embodied First Exam splits 427 of its 456 core tasks into stages (for example, putting a tomato into a closed fridge has three: the fridge is open, the tomato is inside, the fridge is closed again) and labels the stage at which each failed attempt goes wrong; the ten agents failed 6,020 of their 8,473 labeled attempts. Different agents tend to fail a task at the same stage. Pooled over the Standard and Privileged settings, attempts fail at 56% of the material stages they reach (such as wiping or pouring), 39% of the body stages (such as walking or keeping balance) and 17% of the mechanism stages. Stages that need precise actions fail much more often in the Standard Setting, where the agent sees only the robot's sensors. Every run is published with its full trace and a replay: https://www.embodied-first-exam.ai/run/ . Analysis: https://www.embodied-first-exam.ai/blogs/failure-analysis/

## How does the Embodied First Exam differ from other embodied AI benchmarks?

Existing robotics benchmarks are built around visuomotor policy learning. The Embodied First Exam treats the coding agent as the system under test and lets it pick its own control strategy, so it measures agentic robotics ability rather than the quality of a single learned policy. With 1,156 tasks on 47 robots, EFE is more than 20 times larger than other benchmarks of coding agents for robotics, such as RLE-Bench (51 tasks), EmboCoach-Bench (32) and EmbodiedSWE-Bench (28), and it evaluates agents on 456 core tests, against the 7 tasks of CaP-Bench. Earlier embodied evaluation work co-authored by Manling Li includes Embodied Agent Interface (NeurIPS 2024 Oral, https://embodied-agent-interface.github.io/), which evaluates LLMs for embodied decision making with fine-grained error metrics, and EmbodiedBench (ICML 2025 Oral, https://embodiedbench.github.io/), which evaluates multimodal LLMs as vision-driven embodied agents.

## Who made the Embodied First Exam?

Kangrui Wang, Qineng Wang, Changhe Chen, Pingyue Zhang, Chi Gui, Feishi Wang, Canyu Chen, Wenli Xiao, Xiaoyu Huang, Tonghe Zhang, Linjie Li, Zihan Wang, Minyeong Kim, Yiyou Sun, Mingkai Deng, Jinyu Hou, Qi Zhu, Han Liu, Eric P. Xing, Huaxiu Yao, Zhiwen Fan, Yuejiang Liu, Dawn Song, Pieter Abbeel, Li Fei-Fei, Jiajun Wu, Yuke Zhu, Guanya Shi, Ruohan Zhang and Manling Li, from Northwestern University, Carnegie Mellon University, UC Berkeley, University of Washington, Stanford University, UNC-Chapel Hill, Texas A&M University and UT Austin. Guanya Shi, Ruohan Zhang and Manling Li advised the project equally.

## How do I run it or submit an agent?

The code is at https://github.com/mll-lab-nu/embodied-first-exam (it runs on Harbor), with instructions at https://www.embodied-first-exam.ai/run/ and https://www.embodied-first-exam.ai/contribute/. Results are on https://www.embodied-first-exam.ai/leaderboard/.

## Where do agentic robots succeed and fail?

On the 456 core tests of the Embodied First Exam in the Standard Setting, where the agent sees only the robot’s sensors and cannot reset by default, 169 tests (37%) are solved by none of ten coding agents. Failures on a task tend to happen at the same stage for different agents, and stages that change a material or move the robot’s body fail most often once reached (56% and 39%). Using tools is the hardest kind of task and carrying objects the easiest. Many failures come from acting through the robot’s sensors, not from finding a solution: of the 169 unsolved Standard tests, 160 belong to tasks that also have a Privileged test, and some agent solves 122 of those with full simulator state and unlimited resets. Source: https://www.embodied-first-exam.ai/blogs/failure-analysis/

## What information matters to a coding agent controlling a robot?

The exam compares a Standard Setting (sensors only, no resets by default) with a Privileged Setting (full simulator state and unlimited resets). In controlled runs of GPT-6 Astra, adding the exact state of every object raises success from 29% to 45%, while unlimited resets with saved states raise it to 53%; with both it reaches 68%, against 79% in Privileged. At stages that need precise actions, resets recover 36% of failures and exact state 21%, close to a plain second try (19%). Source: https://www.embodied-first-exam.ai/blogs/failure-analysis/

## Do different coding agents solve the same robot tasks?

No. GPT-6 Astra solves 39 Standard tests that Claude Fable 5.2 fails, and Fable solves 108 that Astra fails. GPT-6.1 Sol solves 49 tests that Astra fails, Claude Opus 5.5 46 and Gemini 4 Argon 34. Three runs of GPT-6.1 Sol differ by at most five points in success rate, so a difference of a few tests between two agents is weak evidence. Source: https://www.embodied-first-exam.ai/blogs/failure-analysis/

## Does the harness change how well a coding agent controls robots?

Yes, by up to 7.5 percentage points for the same model: GPT-6 Astra solves 34.4% of the Standard tests in Codex and 27.0% in Claude Code, and Gemini 4 Argon solves 132 tests in Codex against 110 in Antigravity CLI. Source: https://www.embodied-first-exam.ai/blogs/failure-analysis/

## Does spending more help coding agents on robot tasks?

Not by itself. For every agent, the median failed attempt costs more than the median solved one, and GPT-6.1 Sol at medium, high and maximum reasoning effort solves 30.7%, 32.2% and 30.9% of the Standard tests, within run-to-run variation. Source: https://www.embodied-first-exam.ai/blogs/failure-analysis/

## How do coding agents control robots?

In a sample of 2,622 attempts, agents control the robot directly in 60% of Standard attempts but write programs in 94% of Realtime and 82% of Privileged attempts. Given a GPU and a reinforcement-learning library, 25 of 28 soccer tests in the Standard and Realtime settings trained a policy. Source: https://www.embodied-first-exam.ai/blogs/failure-analysis/

## Does the wording of a robot task instruction change the result?

Yes. With RoboDojo’s one-sentence instructions, GPT-6 Astra solves 12 of 54 RoboDojo tasks; with the task recipe and the return-to-start note it solves 33, and with a goal that states the success check in full it solves 37. Source: https://www.embodied-first-exam.ai/blogs/failure-analysis/

## What is Embodied Olympics?

Embodied Olympics is a benchmark in which coding agents build, run and revise the systems that control robots in 18 sports on six simulated robots, from humanoids to a racing drone and a race car. Agents start without supplied motor skills, work within fixed time and compute budgets, and in 16 sports the match keeps running while they reason. Episodic matches start from a fresh workspace; Continual seasons keep code, trained weights and experience. Checkpoint Evaluation replays each agent's first and last program of a match against fixed opponents. Report: https://www.embodied-first-exam.ai/blogs/embodied-olympics/ ; site: https://olympics.embodied-first-exam.ai/

## Can coding agents keep improving their robots through competition?

Mostly not yet. Across seven coding agents, the side with the better first program wins 89 of 98 decisive Episodic matches, because revisions barely change the program: against fixed opponents, revisions within a match gain 0.2 percentage points (3.9 against the current opponent). Agents analyze the opponent correctly in 66% of 515 Episodic seat-matches but field a changed program in 26%, and a change that wins more points in 4%. Over a Continual season, three of six agents improve (Gemini 4 Argon from 16% to 36% of points against fixed opponents, GPT-6 Astra from 34% to 48%, Kimi 3.1 Pro from 6% to 13%). Of 305 self-assessments that claim an improvement, replays confirm 35.

## How far are agent-built robot systems from strong systems?

The strongest agent's programs win 43% of their games against the strongest scripted opponent, and four agents lose all 32 wheeled-soccer matches against the RoboCup Small Size League champions' software without scoring. In badminton, when the shuttle lands out of reach, the robots of the two strongest agents move to it in 2 of 166 and 5 of 142 cases, against 112 of 116 for a scripted practice player.

## Key numbers at a glance

- 1,156 tasks, 35 suites (9 new, 26 adapted from existing benchmarks), 47 robots
- Core set: 456 hard tasks in the paper; 498 on the live leaderboard
- 3 evaluation settings: Standard, Realtime (a variant of Standard), Privileged
- 3 control approaches: direct control, code to control, train a policy to control
- Highest Standard Setting success rate on the paper's 456 core tasks: 50% (ten agents)
